'''Autocrypt''' is a [[cryptographic protocol]] for [[email client]]s aiming to simplify key exchange and enabling [[encryption]]. {{fact|date=December 2019}} Version 1.0 of the [https://autocrypt.org/level1.html Autocrypt specification] was released in December 2017. Version 1.1 was released in January 2019. It is implemented on top of [[OpenPGP]] replacing its complex key management by fully automated exchange of [[Key (cryptography)|cryptographic keys]] between peers {{fact|date=December 2019}}.

== Method ==

Autocrypt-capable email clients transparently negotiate encryption capabilities and preferences and exchange keys between users alongside sending regular emails. {{fact|date=December 2019}} This is done by including the key material and encryption preferences in the header of each email, which allows encrypting any message to a contact who has previously sent the user email. {{fact|date=December 2019}} This information is not signed or verified in any way even if the actual message is encrypted and verified. {{fact|date=December 2019}}

No support is required from [[Mailbox provider|email providers]] other than preserving and not manipulating the Autocrypt specific header fields. {{fact|date=December 2019}}

When a message is encrypted to a group of receivers, keys are also automatically sent to all receivers in this group. This ensures that a reply to a message can be encrypted without any further complications or work by the user. {{fact|date=December 2019}}

== Security model ==

Autocrypt is guided by the idea of opportunistic security from RFC 7435 but implementing something much less secure than a [[trust on first use]] (TOFU) model. Encryption of messages between Autocrypt-capable clients can be enabled without further need of user interaction. {{fact|date=December 2019}} Traditional OpenPGP applications should display a noticeable warning if keys are not verified either manually or by a web of trust method before use. In contrast, Autocrypt completely resigns on any kind of key verification. Key exchange is during the initial handshake and valid or invalid keys of peers may be replaced anytime later without any user interaction or verification. This makes it very easy to exchange new key(s) if a user loses access to the key but also makes the protocol much more susceptible to man-in-the-middle attacks than clean TOFU. The underlying OpenPGP implementation makes it often possible for the user to perform manual out of band key verification, however by design users are never alerted if Autocrypt changed the keys of peers. {{fact|date=December 2019}}

Autocrypt tries to maximize the possible opportunities for encryption, but is not aggressive about encrypting messages at all possible opportunities. Instead, encryption is only enabled by default if all communicating parties consent, allowing users to make themselves available for encrypted communication without getting in the way of their established workflows.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://k9mail.github.io/2018/02/26/OpenPGP-Considerations-Part-III-Autocrypt.html|title=OpenPGP Considerations, Part III: Autocrypt and Encryption by Default {{!}} K-9 Mail|website=k9mail.github.io|language=en|access-date=2018-04-28}}</ref>

[[Man-in-the-middle attack|Man-in-the-middle attacks]] are not preventable in this security model, which is controversial.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.golem.de/news/bye-bye-enigmail-openpgp-wird-in-thunderbird-integriert-1910-144310.html|title=Bye-bye Enigmail!: OpenPGP wird in Thunderbird integriert - Golem.de|website=www.golem.de|language=German|access-date=2019-12-23}}</ref>

Any attacker who can send emails with forged sender-address can cause encryption keys to be replaced by keys of his choice and/or deliberately turn off encryption.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://autocrypt.org/faq.html#what-about-spammers-accidentally-downgrading-encryption|title=Autocrypt FAQ — What about spammers accidentally downgrading encryption?|website=autocrypt.org|access-date=2019-12-01}}</ref>

== Technical details ==

Autocrypt uses the established OpenPGP specification as its underlying data format. 
With Version 1.1 support for [[Elliptic Curve Cryptography]] (ECC) has been introduced and is the standard for new keys, because it provides the same security with shorter keys.<ref>{{cite web|access-date=2025-01-02 |title=Autocrypt Level 1: Enabling encryption, avoiding annoyances |url=https://docs.autocrypt.org/level1.html#openpgp-based-key-data}}<!-- auto-translated from German by Module:CS1 translator --></ref> For this [[Curve25519]] is used.<ref>{{cite web|access-date=2025-01-02 |title=Autocrypt FAQ Frequently Asked Questions |url=https://docs.autocrypt.org/faq.html#why-also-rsa3072-and-not-only-curve-25519-keys}}<!-- auto-translated from German by Module:CS1 translator --></ref>
Messages are encrypted using [[Advanced Encryption Standard|AES]] and [[RSA (cryptosystem)|RSA]] keys, with a recommended RSA key length of 3072 bits. These mechanisms are chosen for maximum compatibility with existing OpenPGP implementations. There are plans for moving to smaller [[Elliptic-curve cryptography|Elliptic-curve]] keys when support is more widely available.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://autocrypt.org/faq.html#why-rsa3072-and-25519-only-later|title=Autocrypt FAQ — Why RSA3072 and 25519 only later?|website=autocrypt.org|access-date=2018-04-29}}</ref>

The <code>Autocrypt</code> header field features a <code>tag=value</code> format common to several mechanisms (for example [[DomainKeys Identified Mail#Technical details|dkim]]), where the <code>keydata</code> tag contains the public key.  It is similar to an armored key export, except that it misses the <code>-----BEGIN PGP PUBLIC KEY BLOCK-----</code> and <code>-----END PGP PUBLIC KEY BLOCK-----</code> lines.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://autocrypt.org/level1.html#the-autocrypt-header|title=The Autocrypt Header|website=autocrypt.org|access-date=2024-05-29}}</ref>

For example:
<syntaxhighlight lang="email">
Autocrypt: addr=alice@autocrypt.example; prefer-encrypt=mutual; keydata=
 mDMEXEcE6RYJKwYBBAHaRw8BAQdArjWwk3FAqyiFbFBKT4TzXcVBqPTB3gmzlC/Ub7O1u12
 0F2FsaWNlQGF1dG9jcnlwdC5leGFtcGxliJYEExYIAD4WIQTrhbtfozp14V6UTmPyMVUMT0
 fjjgUCXEcE6QIbAwUJA8JnAAULCQgHAgYVCgkICwIEFgIDAQIeAQIXgAAKCRDyMVUMT0fjj
 kqLAP9frlijw BJvA+HFnqCZcYIVxlyXzS5Gi5gMTpp37K73jgD/VbKYhkwk9iu689OYH4K
 7q7LbmdeaJ+RX88Y/ ad9hZwy4OARcRwTpEgorBgEEAZdVAQUBAQdAQv8GIa2rSTzgqbXCp
 DDYMiKRVitCsy203x3sE9+eviIDAQgHiHgEGBYIACAWIQTrhbtfozp14V6UTmPyMVUMT0fj
 jgUCXEcE6QIbDAAKCRDyMVUMT0fjjlnQAQDFHUs6TIcxrNTtEZFjUFm1M0PJ1Dng/cDW4xN
 80fsn0QEA22Kr7VkCjeAEC08VSTeV+QFsmz55/lntWkwYWhmvOgE=
</syntaxhighlight>

==  Support ==
* [[Kontact]] since version 21.04.<ref>{{cite web|title=KDE Gear 21.04 released|url=https://kde.org/announcements/gear/21.04/|accessdate=2021-04-22|first1=Paul|last1=Brown|first2=Carl|last2=Schwan|first3=Áron|last3=Kovács|date=22 April 2021}}</ref>{{fact|date=January 2022}}
* [[Delta Chat|Delta Chat messenger]] from Version 0.9.2.<ref>{{cite web|title=Delta Chat v0.9.2 feat. Autocrypt Level 1|url=https://delta.chat/en/2017-06-28-delta-chat-0-9-2|accessdate=2018-04-26}}</ref> 
* [[K-9 Mail]] Android mail-app has support since Version 5.400<ref>{{cite web|title=5.4 Release {{!}} K-9 Mail|url=https://k9mail.github.io/2018/01/07/5.4-Release.html|accessdate=2018-04-24|archive-date=21 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181221182722/https://k9mail.github.io/2018/01/07/5.4-Release.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> (reportedly broken until version 5.717<ref>{{cite web|url=https://github.com/k9mail/k-9/issues/3451#issuecomment-655144999|title=K-9 mail fails to encrypt emails by default, even with "Autocrypt mutual mode" enabled|website=[[GitHub]]|accessdate=2021-02-27}}</ref>).
* SnappyMail webmail from Version 2.34.0.<ref>{{cite web|title=Releases: the-djmaze/snappymail|website=[[GitHub]] |url=https://github.com/the-djmaze/snappymail/releases|accessdate=2024-02-17}}</ref>
* [[Mozilla Thunderbird|Thunderbird]] partially supports AutoCrypt since version 78.  Thunderbird generates, sends and receives AutoCrypt headers, but does not automatically install received public keys.  User action is still required to approve and install a sender's public key.<ref>{{cite web |date=26 June 2022 |title=Does Thunderbird support Autocrypt? |url=https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/openpgp-thunderbird-howto-and-faq#w_does-thunderbird-support-autocrypt |accessdate=2024-06-25 |website=Mozilla Support}}</ref>
* The German email provider [[Posteo]] supports AutoCrypt, and improves its security by also cryptographically signing outbound Autocrypt header data via [[DomainKeys_Identified_Mail|DKIM]].<ref>{{cite web |date=18 December 2017 |title=Vereinfachte E-Mail-Verschlüsselung mit Autocrypt- und OpenPGP-Header |url=https://posteo.de/blog/neu-vereinfachte-e-mail-verschl%C3%BCsselung-mit-autocrypt-und-openpgp-header |accessdate=2018-04-24 |website=Posteo.de |language=German |quote= |trans-quote=Our contribution to security: We additionally secure the key exchange with Autocrypt with digital signatures (DKIM). This is not currently provided as standard with Autocrypt. Our provider-side DKIM signature ensures that public keys cannot be manipulated unnoticed during transport. We also sign Autocrypt headers that your local email program may add with DKIM. The signature is applied if the sender matches the mailbox. We save the key exchange with Autocrypt additionally with digital signatures (DKIM). This is not yet provided by default at Autocrypt. Our provider-side DKIM signing ensures that public keys cannot be manipulated unnoticed on transport. We also sign autocrypt header, which your local email program may add, with DKIM. The signature is made when the sender matches the mailbox.}}</ref>
* No longer functional: Autocrypt extension in Thunderbird.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://addons.thunderbird.net/en-US/thunderbird/addon/autocrypt/|title=Autocrypt|website=addons.thunderbird.net|language=en-US|access-date=2019-10-08}}</ref>
* No longer functional: [[Mozilla Thunderbird|Thunderbird]] extension [[Enigmail]] since version 2.0.<ref>{{cite web|title=Enigmail - 2018-03-25 Enigmail v2.0 released|url=https://enigmail.net/index.php/en/home/news/63-2018-03-25-enigmail-v2-0-released|accessdate=2018-04-24|last=Patrick Brunschwig}}</ref>
